Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:6: And the reason Scripture calls Israel brothers and fellows, saying (Leviticus 25:25), "if your brother becomes poor," and "and you shall love your neighbor" (ibid. 19:18), and many similar cases, is to allude that just as a mother who bore two males, they are called brothers because both were in one womb, and where one was, the other was too - this is the relation of brotherhood, even though the bodies are separate in their existence. And brotherhood applies even more truly if they were born twins, for both were as one in one womb and were born as one. And along these lines, there is a spiritual place above called by the term "womb" [rechem], the place where souls are conceived, as it says (Exodus 13:2), "sanctify to Me every firstborn, whatever opens the womb," as explained in the Zohar, Parashat Bereishit (page 13b), the commandment of laying tefillin; see there. And of this it is also said (Habakkuk 3:2), "in wrath, remember mercy [rachem]" - and there, in the conception of souls, six hundred thousand are in one womb and born as one - it follows, from this aspect, that all Israel are brothers, and doubly brothers - since all of them were as one in one place, along the lines of twin brothers - this is a great unification for the souls from the aspect of their spirituality. And of this Job said (Job 31:15), "did not He who made me in the belly make him? And did not the same One form us in the womb?" - and he mentioned two aspects, "belly" and "womb," for so it is above too (ibid. 38:29), "from whose belly comes the ice?" - as my teacher, peace be upon him, explained in the Gate of the Meanings of Terms (Pardes, section 23, on "belly").
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:7: And the aspect of love from the side of the body is that he should think that since we are all fashioned by one Craftsman in His image, as it is said (Genesis 9:6), "in the image of God He made man," it follows that whoever disgraces his fellow disgraces himself. And moreover, as it were, he disgraces the Craftsman who made him - and for this our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in Bereishit Rabbah (24:7): Ben Azzai says, "this is the book of the generations of Adam" (Genesis 5:1) - this is a great principle of the Torah. Rabbi Akiva says, "and you shall love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18) - this is a great principle of the Torah, so that you should not say, since I have been disgraced, let my fellow be disgraced too, since I have been cursed, let my fellow be cursed with me. Rabbi Tanchuma said, if you do so, know whom you disgrace: "in the likeness of God He made him" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:8: Further, it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Miketz, page 201a) that when Israel are with one another in love, they cause the side of the right and Chesed to be drawn to the world, as it is written (Jeremiah 31:2), "with an everlasting love I have loved you, therefore I have drawn you with kindness [chesed]" - and if not, God forbid, the left prevails, for hatred is drawn from the left, and the external force, drawn from the left, is completed and its "measure of stature" becomes whole. These are its words: it opened and said, "do not say, I will repay evil," and so on (Proverbs 20:22). Come and see, the Holy One, blessed be He, made a person so that he strengthen himself with Torah and walk in the path of truth and the side of the right, and not walk to the side of the left - and because they need to walk to the side of the right, they must increase love with one another, and there should be no enmity between them, so as not to weaken the right, which is the place Israel cling to. And come and see, because of this there are the good inclination and the evil inclination, and Israel need to strengthen the good inclination over the evil inclination through proper deeds - and if a person strays to the left, then the evil inclination is strengthened over the good inclination, and whoever was blemished completes it through his sins, for this loathsome one is completed only through people's sins - and therefore a person must be careful that this evil inclination not be completed through his sins, and guard himself constantly, for the good inclination wishes to complete him constantly, not the evil inclination - and therefore, "do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the LORD, and He shall save you."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:9: Another explanation: "do not say, I will repay evil" - as it is written (Psalms 38:21), "and those who repay evil for good" - for one who has repaid him good, he should not repay evil, because of the fear of the Holy One, blessed be He, along the lines of (Genesis 42:18), "do this and live," and so on - and He too always acts this way, as it is written (Proverbs 17:13), "whoever repays evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house" - even if they repaid him evil, he must not repay evil for the evil they repaid him, but rather, "wait for the LORD, and He shall save you" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:10: Further, among the things a person should think in order not to come to quarrel with his fellow is what the Tanna said in Avot, chapter 2 (mishnah 4), "do not judge your fellow until you reach his place." And the pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz, peace be upon him, wrote in his commentary on this mishnah, and it further appears to me, that this is a great principle for the endurance of peace and love among people - since most of the quarrels that occur among people are caused by a person judging one standard for himself and another standard for others - and therefore it warned, "do not judge your fellow until you reach his place," so that your mind and soul be under his soul. For example: a person disgraced you over something you did to him - do not respond until you yourself judge whether, had he done to you what you did to him, you would have disgraced him even more than he disgraced you. And likewise, the same parable applies to any business dealing you have with your fellow: if you are owed by him, think in your mind whether, were it the reverse, what you would want him to do to you, and equalize yourself to him as well. In sum, this is a great principle for increasing peace in the world - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:11: Further, whoever regards his fellow with a good eye shall not quickly be filled with anger against him - and so the pious author mentioned wrote, on the mishnah (Avot, chapter 2, mishnah 10), "Rabbi Eliezer says, let your fellow's honor be as dear to you as your own, and be not easily angered" - these are its words: all these warnings are a preparation for attaining wisdom, for the acquisition of a companion is a great aid in learning Torah, as it said, "and acquire for yourself a companion," and all the more so in being precise about companions. And be careful of the honor of companions, for through this their companionship shall endure, and they shall have good reward for their toil - and in the commentary on "acquire for yourself a companion" I have written of this with the help of Heaven. And its saying "be not easily angered," to me, is because of the lightness of anger and its swiftness, in proportion to the good deeds received by the one against whom the anger is directed, from the angry one - and therefore the quarrel between relatives always grows greater, and the Name, blessed be He, is exacting with His pious ones to a hair's breadth, since they have received more of true success - and therefore it warned, even though you are careful of your fellow's honor and have not sinned against him while he sinned against you, be not easily angered. And when you examine it well, you shall find this teaching flowing from his own attribute, peace be upon him, which is a good eye - for whoever regards people with an evil eye fills his belly with people's faults, and with a small cause, like new wineskins, he bursts, as it says (Ecclesiastes 7:9), "for anger rests in the bosom of fools" - for because of the lightness and swiftness of their anger, it is as though it pitched its tent there; if so, the swiftness of anger reveals the disgrace of its owner. But whoever is slow to anger indicates in his own soul that he regards matters with a good eye, and therefore does not quickly become angry - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:12: Further, among the things that nullify hatred and anger is the matter of rebuke - that he rebuke his fellow and say, why did you do such-and-such to me - and it is possible that his fellow shall excuse himself to him, as we find Abraham our father, peace be upon him, did with Abimelech, as it is said (Genesis 21:25), "and Abraham rebuked Abimelech concerning the well of water that Abimelech's servants had seized" - and he excused himself to him, as it is said, "and Abimelech said, I did not know who did this thing," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:13: And they said in Bereishit Rabbah (54:3), on this verse "and Abraham rebuked," and so on: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina said, rebuke leads to love, as it is said (Proverbs 9:8), "rebuke a wise man and he will love you" - this is the view of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina, who said, any love without rebuke is not love. Reish Lakish said, rebuke leads to peace: "and Abraham rebuked Abimelech" - this is his view, who said, any peace without rebuke is not peace - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:14: And for this the Torah commanded (Leviticus 19:17), "you shall not hate your brother in your heart; you shall surely rebuke your fellow, and not bear sin because of him." And so Ramban, peace be upon him, explained this verse - these are its words: and what appears correct to me is that "you shall surely rebuke" is like "and Abraham rebuked Abimelech" - and Scripture says, "you shall not hate your brother in your heart" when he does to you against your will, but rather you shall rebuke him, why have you done thus to me, "and not bear sin because of him" by covering his hatred in your heart and not telling him - for by rebuking him he shall excuse himself to you, or shall return and confess his sin and you shall forgive him - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:15: And since the matter of rebuke has come to our hand, let us say something of it, for it is a positive commandment - and first we shall copy the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, since they follow the plain sense - these are its words, in Parashat Kedoshim (page 85b), in explaining the verse - the Ra'aya Meheimna: this is the commandment to rebuke one who has sinned, to show him abundant love that one loves him, and so that he not be punished - for of the Holy One, blessed be He, it is written (Proverbs 3:12), "for whom the LORD loves, He rebukes" - and because the Holy One, blessed be He, rebukes whoever He loves, a person shall learn from that way and rebuke his fellow. How does the Holy One, blessed be He, rebuke a person? He rebukes him with love, in private - if he accepts it, good; if not, He rebukes him among his loved ones - if he accepts it, good; if not, He rebukes him openly, before the eyes of all - if he accepts it, good; if not, He leaves him and does not rebuke him, and lets him go and do as he wishes. At first, He makes it known to him privately, in order to rebuke him and arouse him, so that no one shall know of it - and this is between him and Him alone - if he accepts it, good; if not, He makes it known among his loved ones - at the time the High Priest was in the world, [Heaven] would give him illnesses upon his bed, and the loved ones of the Holy One, blessed be He, would come and make known to him whether there was a sin in him that he should repent from, and examine his own conduct - if he accepts it, good; if not, He rebukes him openly, in his wealth, in his children, that everyone whispers about him and they come to him - if he accepts it, good; if not, his Master leaves him to do his own will and shall never seize him again. In this manner one must rebuke his fellow: first privately, then among his loved ones, then openly - from then on, he shall leave him and let him do his own will. And therefore it is written "you shall surely rebuke" [hoche'ach tochi'ach] - "hoche'ach" privately, so that no one know of it; "tochi'ach" among his loved ones and friends; "your fellow" openly - and therefore it does not say first "tochi'ach," but "hoche'ach" and then "tochi'ach." If it is a person who would be ashamed, he should not tell him and rebuke him even privately, but should say before him, as though speaking of other matters, and within those words mention that whoever did that sin is thus and so - since he himself knows [it refers to him] and shall desist from that sin - and this is "hoche'ach," and if not, "tochi'ach," and afterward "your fellow" openly - from then on, "and you shall not bear sin because of him" - for once a person rebukes his fellow and comes to rebuke him openly, he should not raise before him that sin he committed, which is certainly forbidden to him, but should speak in general terms and not raise that sin openly against him, nor mark a sin against him - for the Holy One, blessed be He, has regard for a person's honor even among the guilty - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:16: And in Arachin (16b, per the reading of "ad") they said: one might think, even if his face changes color [from shame] - therefore Scripture says, "and you shall not bear sin because of him." Rabbi Tarfon said, I wonder if there is anyone in this generation capable of rebuking. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya said, by the [divine] service, I wonder if there is anyone in this generation capable of accepting rebuke. Rabbi Akiva said, by the [divine] service, I wonder if there is anyone in this generation who knows how to rebuke - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:17: And in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu (Rabbah, chapter 18), copied in the Yalkut, in the explanation of the verse (Parashat Vayikra, remez 613): another explanation, "your people who are with you" - with mitzvot you rebuke, but you do not rebuke a wicked person who might hate you, as it is said (Proverbs 9:7), "he who corrects a scoffer gets shame for himself" - for he himself has a blemish - to this point. Rabbi Elazar ben Matya says, if there is a matter between you and him, tell it to him, and do not sin through it - therefore it is said, "and not bear sin because of him." Similarly you say (Proverbs 24:17), "do not rejoice when your enemy falls," and elsewhere it says (ibid. 11:10), "and at the destruction of the wicked, there is joyous song" - how can these two verses be reconciled? A Torah scholar who bested you today in halachah, and a matter [befalling him unfortunately] comes to hand tomorrow, do not rejoice over it, lest the LORD see and it be evil in His eyes [i.e., displease Him] - but if you see a person in Israel who desires his fellow's harm, this is a wholly wicked person - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:18: And in Bava Metzia (31a) it says: "hoche'ach" [rebuke] implies even a hundred times; "tochi'ach" - I know only of a teacher toward a student; a student toward a teacher, from where? Scripture says "tochi'ach" in any case - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:19: Concerning the reward of the one who rebukes and the one who accepts rebuke, they, of blessed memory, said in Tractate Tamid (28a), on the verse (Proverbs 24:25), "but to those who rebuke it shall be pleasant, and a blessing of good shall come upon them" - it is taught, Rabbi says, what is the straight path a person should choose for himself? To love rebuke - for as long as rebuke exists in the world, there is contentment in the world, goodness and blessing come to the world, and evil departs from the world, as it is said, "but to those who rebuke it shall be pleasant." And some say, he shall hold fast to abundant faithfulness, as it is said (Psalms 101:6), "my eyes are on the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with me." Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, whoever rebukes his fellow for the sake of Heaven merits a portion of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said (Proverbs 28:23), "he who rebukes a man, after [him]" - and moreover, a thread of kindness is drawn toward him, as it is said, "shall find favor" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:20: And in Eleh HaDevarim Rabbah, at the beginning of the parashah - these are its words: another explanation, "these are the words" - our Rabbis say, the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses, since they have accepted your rebuke, you must bless them - from where? As it is said (Deuteronomy 1:10), "the LORD your God has multiplied you," and so on - and from where do we know that whoever accepts rebuke merits blessing? For so Solomon spells out, "but to those who rebuke it shall be pleasant, and a blessing of good shall come upon them" - to this point. And the intent of saying "for so Solomon spells out" is to make us understand the precision of Solomon's words, that the word "upon them" [aleihem] at first glance is superfluous if it refers back to "those who rebuke" - so Solomon explained it and said "and upon them," to indicate those who accept the rebuke, who merit blessing.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:21: Further, matters to be saved from anger, Rabbi Yitzchak of Acre, peace be upon him, wrote in his book - these are its words: one of the nights, on Sabbath eve, I was thinking about what a person should do so as not to become angry, and I began to doze off, and while dozing I felt as though someone said to me, whoever wishes not to be an angry person should be intelligent - and the explanation of "intelligent" is that he should follow the essence of the matter and the essence of the words, and not set his heart and mind on what his eyes see or his ears hear of the things done or said to him to anger him, and pay no attention to them at all, but strive after the essence - meaning, after the merit of the one who says or does them: if he sees that the one saying or doing them is a fool and a boor, immediately his mind and the boiling of his anger shall cool; and if he is wise and intelligent, likewise the boiling of his anger shall cool - for if he is a fool, he shall think of him and say, this one is a fool without sense, and his words are not with intelligence, and his words are nothing but chirping like the chirping of birds, or like the barking of a dog and the braying of a donkey. And of the wise man he shall think and recognize that he speaks for his own good and benefit, and shall accept his words from him and rejoice in them - and he should not look at the things said to him nor at the deeds done to anger him, but only at the merit of the one who says or does them. However, if the things or deeds are unfitting or improper, whether they come from the very one who said or did them, or a wise or foolish man brings them up to him, he should not look at the one bringing them up, but only at the deeds themselves, since he recognizes that they are true, that he said them or did them - and great benefit shall come to him from this, for he shall repair his own attributes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:22: Further, I shall let you hear a good counsel to ease anger and restrain it: when you have a business dealing with a person who is not good, let there be a complete agreement settled in your heart, to endure from him every kind of insult in word and deed - for when a person expects his fellow to insult him in word and deed, it shall not come upon him suddenly and he shall not become angry - do so until you are free of him, then flee from him like a goring ox in the month of Nisan, and through this your life shall be a good life - to this point, although I have shortened it somewhat as fits our purpose.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:23: Further, among the things that bring a person to submission and the nullification of anger, the pious author of Chovot HaLevavot wrote (Gate of Submission, chapter 5), that one of them is when he thinks of his own passing, and that death shall come to him swiftly, cutting off his desires and hopes, and the form of his standing among the graves. And the second is when what he owes in divine service, for the abundance of His kindnesses toward him and the greatness of His goodness, passes over a person's heart, and his neglect of the commandments of hearing and reason and his falling short in them, and the cutting off of his arguments and excuses on the day of reckoning, and his remorse at the moment of recompense - he shall submit and break his own spirit, as it is said (Malachi 3:19), "for behold, the day comes, burning like a furnace," and so on, "and who can endure the day of His coming?" (ibid. 3:2).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:24: And the matter of these aspects is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Miketz, page 201b), on the verse (Genesis 43:18), "and the men were afraid because they were brought to Joseph's house" - these are its words: Rabbi Yosei says, woe to people who do not know and do not consider the ways of Torah - woe to them at the hour the Holy One, blessed be He, comes to demand of them judgment for their deeds, and body and soul shall arise to give an account of all their deeds, before the spirit separates from the body - and that day of judgment is the day the books are opened and the masters of judgment stand, for at that time the serpent stands ready to bite him, and all his limbs are stirred toward him, and the soul separates from the body and goes and wanders, not knowing which way to go nor where it shall ascend - woe to that day, a day of wrath and distress, that day. Therefore a person must arouse his own inclination every day, and remind himself of that day he shall stand in judgment, when they bring him under the earth to decay, and his soul separates from him. And we have learned, a person should always arouse the good inclination against the evil inclination and pursue it - if it departs from him, good, and if not, let him occupy himself with Torah, for there is nothing that breaks the evil inclination but Torah; if it departs, better, and if not, let him remind himself of the day of death, in order to break it - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:25: And it said further shortly after: and therefore a person must always be aroused by that great day, the day of judgment, the day of reckoning, for a person has nothing to shield him except his own proper deeds that he does in this world, so that they may shield him at that hour - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:26: And when a person takes to heart that his Creator is angry with him over his pride and anger, and all his deeds are written in a book, and his sin is not quickly erased, as it is written (Jeremiah 17:1), "the sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, with the point of a diamond," as explained in the Gate of Repentance (chapter 5) - how ashamed and humiliated he shall be in the future, when he sees his deeds engraved before him, and how shall he not be ashamed, that it be proclaimed above, so-and-so worshipped idolatry, and the other blemish he has blemished his soul with.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:27: And further, there is nothing that nullifies cleaving [to God] more than anger, and therefore Rabbi So-and-so said, on the day I was enraged I did not pray (Eruvin 65a) - and a person's being made in a supernal image, as explained in the Gate of Holiness, is that he cleave to the Name, blessed be He, through the holy soul - this is what King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 8:6), "and You have made him a little lower than the angels, and crowned him with glory and honor" - and this "honor" [hadar] is the honor of the beard [zaken], whose allusion is in the supernal place, as explained in the Idra of Naso (page 134a) - and it said, "You made him rule over the works of Your hands; You have put all things under his feet: sheep and oxen, all of them," and so on - and through anger, the soul departs from him, and what had been above everything remains beneath everything, in the husk, as explained above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:28: Further, among the things that nullify anger, the author of Chovot HaLevavot wrote (Gate of Submission, chapter 7), and said that when people speak of his own disgrace, if they mention a deed he did, he should confess his own shortcoming and not go seeking excuses to clear himself of it and vindicate himself, as Judah said (Genesis 38:26), "she is more righteous than I." And he should not strive to shame the one telling of it, nor accuse him for having revealed it, but rather say to him, my brother, how small is what you have observed of my evil deeds compared to what you do not know of me, which the Creator has prolonged in concealing - for had my evil deeds and sins been revealed to you, you would have fled from me - and he shall submit to the Creator and thank Him for having revealed a little of the much, to discipline him so that he return to Him. And if what was told of him is false, the one who says it loses his own merits - and it was already said of one of the pious ones, that they spoke ill of him, and when the matter reached him, he sent to the one who had spoken of him a vessel filled with the choicest produce of the land, and wrote to him, it has reached me that you sent me a gift from your own merits, and I have repaid you for this. And one of the pious ones said, many people shall come on the day of reckoning, and when they are shown their deeds, they shall find in the book of their merits, merits they did not do, and they shall say, we did not do these - and they shall be told, so-and-so did them, who spoke of you and told of your disgrace. And likewise, when the merits of those who spoke of their disgrace are diminished in their own books, they shall seek them at that time, and they shall be told, they were lost from you at the time you spoke of so-and-so and so-and-so. And likewise, some of them shall find in their book of debts, debts they did not incur, and when they say, we did not incur these, they shall be told, they were added to you because of so-and-so and so-and-so, whom you spoke of - as it is said (Psalms 79:12), "and return to our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom," and so on - to this point. And some of his words we have skipped, so as not to be lengthy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:29: And concerning this aspect of added merit that he mentioned, it appears to me that this is why David, whom Shimi ben Gera disgraced (II Samuel 16:11), said, "leave him alone, and let him curse, for the LORD has told him. Perhaps the LORD will look upon my affliction, and the LORD will repay me good for his cursing this day." And "good" means the merits [good deeds] of Shimi shall be transferred to David in place of the curse he cursed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:30: Further, among the causes that nullify anger is when one considers how many corruptions are drawn from anger - for whoever becomes suddenly angry and does not restrain his temper comes to bloodshed, as it says in Sefer Chasidim (siman 655): there was a story of a son who honored his father exceedingly. The father said to him, you honor me in my life - honor me in my death: I command you to hold back your anger for one night and restrain your spirit from speaking. After his father's passing, he went to a land across the sea and left his wife pregnant without knowing it, and he was delayed on the road for several years - and when he returned to the city, he came at night and went up to the room where his wife was lying, and he heard the voice of a young man kissing her. He drew his sword and wished to kill them both, but he remembered his father's command and returned it to its sheath. He heard her say to that young man, her son who was with her, it has already been many years since your father left me - had he known that a son was born to him, he would already have arranged a wife for you. When he heard this, he said, "open for me, my sister, my beloved" - blessed is the LORD who let my anger pass, and blessed is my father who commanded me to restrain my anger for one night, that I not kill you and my son - and they rejoiced with great joy, and so on - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:31: And in the first chapter of Gittin (6b) they, of blessed memory, said: Rav Chisda said, a person should never cast excessive fear within his household, for the concubine at Giv'ah - her husband cast excessive fear upon her, and this caused the fall of many myriads of Israel.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:32: Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav, whoever casts excessive fear within his household eventually comes to three transgressions: forbidden relations, bloodshed, and desecration of the Sabbath - to this point. And Rashi explained: "forbidden relations" - when her time for immersion arrives during cold weather, and she is afraid to say, I have not immersed, and has relations with him while a menstruant. "Bloodshed" - if he strikes her, or sometimes she flees from him and falls into a pit or off a bridge. "And desecration of Sabbaths" - sometimes she lights a lamp or cooks after nightfall out of fear of him, and he does not know - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:33: Rabbah bar bar Chanah said, that which the Rabbis said (Shabbat, chapter 2, mishnah 7), three things a person must say in his household on the eve of the Sabbath, and so on - have you tithed? Have you prepared the eruv? Light the lamp! - he must say them calmly, so that they be accepted from him. Rav Ashi said, I had not heard this teaching of Rabbah bar bar Chanah, but arrived at it through my own reasoning.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:34: Rabbi Abahu said, a person should never cast excessive fear within his household, for a great man cast excessive fear within his household - and who was he? Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel - and they sought to feed him a limb from a living animal - to this point. And Rashi explained that they had lost the limb from the slaughtered animal, and out of fear of him they cut a limb from a living animal and brought it in its place so that he not notice - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:35: And when a person considers the secret of a man and his wife in their supernal allusion, that they allude to the secret of the supernal Cherubim - when there is peace between them, they are a chariot for the supernal place, for the attribute of peace is what unifies above - and if there is no peace between them, woe to them, for they display separation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:36: And in Pirkei Rabbi Eliezer (chapter 11) it says - these are its words: and once He built for him a helper, a woman, he was called "ish" [man] and she "ishah" [woman] - what did the Holy One, blessed be He, do? He placed His own Name between them, Yud-Hei: if they walk in My ways and keep My commandments, behold My Name is placed between them and saves them from all trouble; and if not, behold I remove My Name from between them, and they become fire and fire, and fire consumes fire, as it is said (Job 31:12), "for it is a fire that consumes until destruction" - to this point. And although this teaching is inclusive of all mitzvot and all transgressions, the matter of anger in particular is the great cause of the departure of the Shechinah from between them, for anger comes from the bile and the liver, which is fire, and as it is written in the Tikkunim (page 85a), whoever becomes angry is as though he kindled the fire of Gehinnom - and therefore, since they quarrel in anger, they become fire and fire, and then it is fire, and then that fire "consumes until destruction," as the teaching of the Tikkunim states.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:37: And therefore the Torah commanded that a person conduct himself within his household with joy, as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Va'etchanan, page 269) - these are its words: "and you shall speak of them" - it should say "and you shall speak," but rather a person must conduct himself by them, and conduct himself so as not to stray right or left. "When you sit in your house" - to conduct himself in his house in the straight way and in the way of proper order, that the people of his household learn from him, to conduct himself with them calmly and joyfully, and not cast excessive fear upon the people of his household, and all his deeds in his house shall be in the way of proper order - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:38: And whoever is proud toward the people of his household is not accepted in their eyes, and the prophet Habakkuk (2:5) called him "a proud man" - and so they expounded in Bava Batra (98a): Rav Yosef said, learn from this that this one who is proud is not accepted even by the people of his own household, as it is said, "a proud man, and he shall not abide" - in his own abode - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:39: And in Midrash Tehillim, on the psalm "I will sing of kindness and judgment" (Psalms 101:1), on the verse (verse 7), "he shall not dwell within my house" - Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, a person must be insulted [and not insult] within his own household - and if within his own household he must be insulted, all the more so within the house of the Holy One, blessed be He.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:40: And if his wife rebukes him in matters of Heaven, he is obligated to accept it from her, and this is one of the ways of humility - and if she sees something improper in him and does not rebuke him, she is punished - for so we find the wife of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon was punished, because she did not protest against him, as they said in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah (18a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:41: Now, most of the quarrels that occur between a man and his wife are caused by the loss of money, such as when his wine or oil is spilled and the like - and of this they said (Ta'anit 20b) concerning the merit of Rav Adda, who lived long because he was never exacting within his household. And so they further expounded in the Midrash Bamidbar Rabbah, Parashat Ki Tisa (9:2) - these are their words: another explanation, "ish ish" [a man, a man] - the Torah has taught you to be yielding in your household: your wine spilled? Be yielding, to leave an inheritance; and likewise your oil, "and I shall fill their treasuries." Your garment was torn? "The LORD shall fulfill all your requests." But if you hear a bad word from your wife, "rise up like a man [gever]" - to whom you are superior [gaver], be a man [gever] - therefore it says "ish ish" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:42: And besides the fact that one who is yielding with his money lives long, as explained above, his sins are also atoned - for so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in Sanhedrin (102b) concerning Achav: Rav Yosef said, Achav was yielding with his money, and because he benefited Torah scholars from his possessions, half his sins were atoned - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:43: And so, similarly, if an incident occurs between a person and his fellow, that money was lost through negligence - if it is a small amount, he should forgive and not force it to court over a small amount, and think that a person does not even bruise his finger below unless it is proclaimed against him from above (Chullin 7b), and this is included among sufferings, and it is fitting to accept them with a pleasant countenance. And if it is a matter of great loss, and the matter concerns the court, he should not soil his mouth with complaints against his fellow, litigation, curses, and the like, and should enter with every person beyond the letter of the law, as we say in the chapter "Elu Metziot" (Bava Metzia 30b): Rav Yosef taught, "and you shall make known to them" (Exodus 18:20) - this is the house of their lives [livelihood]; "the way" - this is acts of kindness; "in which they shall walk" - this is visiting the sick; "in it" - this is burial; "and the deed" - this is judgment; "that they shall do" - this is beyond the letter of the law. And it said shortly after, Rabbi said, Jerusalem was destroyed only because they based their judgments on strict Torah law and did not act beyond the letter of the law.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:44: And at the end of the chapter "Ha'Umanin" (Bava Metzia 83a), they, of blessed memory, said: certain porters broke a barrel of wine belonging to Rabbah bar bar Chanan, and he seized their cloaks [as compensation]. They came and told Rav. He said to him, give them back their cloaks. He said to him, is this the law? He said to him, yes - "that you may walk in the way of good men" (Proverbs 2:20). He gave them back their cloaks. They said to him, we are poor, and we have toiled all day and are hungry, and we have nothing. He said to him, go, give them their wages. He said to him, is this the law? He said to him, yes - "and keep the paths of the righteous" - to this point. And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained "in the way of good men" as beyond the letter of the law. Behold, when a person considers this deed, several instances of anger and quarrel shall be removed from him, from what is between him and his fellow, between him and other people, and from his own household - quarrels people are accustomed to become exacting over because they do not wish to act beyond the letter of the law.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:45: And even if they rob something from him, it is fitting that he forgive it, when it is impossible to recover it through the courts, so that his fellow not be punished and burden the Holy One, blessed be He, to bring about a chain of circumstances until the money reaches his hand - along the lines of what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained on the verse (Deuteronomy 1:17), "you shall not be afraid of any man, for the judgment is God's" - the Holy One, blessed be He, says, it is not enough for the wicked that they take money from one and give it to another, but they also burden Me to return the money to its owner - to this point, Yalkut, Parashat Va'eleh HaDevarim, in explaining the verse (remez 802).
